source.title: Principal Components Bias in Deep Neural Networks

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; the supplied title is a shortened variant of the paper title.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests the random-label convergence claim in linear and nonlinear networks, but its main method studies learning curves and compares convergence under natural, shuffled, and whitened labels rather than reproducing the original random-label memorization setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports learning-curve comparisons for true and shuffled labels in Figs. 9 and 10. It does not report the random-label training-error and test-error-at-chance result required by V1, nor tests shuffled pixels, independent pixel permutations, Gaussian inputs, the complete sweep of corrupted-label fractions, regularization and augmentation under random labels, or real-versus-random learning order as in Arpit et al. Table 1 concerns discriminability and accessibility, not any claim version.
record.test_reason: Section 6 directly compares convergence with original and shuffled labels in SGD-trained two-layer linear networks, bearing on V2. It does not establish random-label interpolation in standard nonlinear deep networks. Figure 10 uses deliberately structured replacement labels rather than completely random labels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the Section 6 conclusions: PC-bias explains the observed shuffled-label slowdown in deep linear networks, whitening removes that slowdown, and constructed nonlinear tasks are learned faster when discrimination requires fewer leading principal components. These findings do not establish arbitrary random-label interpolation or its numerical training-time cost.
record.recipe_differences: The paper examines principal-component effects on learning dynamics; it compares true and shuffled labels and uses whitening or constructed datasets rather than reproducing random-label memorization and measuring chance test error.
record.method_sensitivity: Whitening changes the relative convergence rate for shuffled labels: the natural-image slowdown disappears after ZCA whitening. In the constructed nonlinear datasets, learning speed varies with the number P of discriminative principal components.

fits_no_version.finding: Nonlinear st-VGG networks learn the constructed datasets faster when fewer leading principal components suffice for classification, for both original-derived and shuffled-derived labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning speed depends on which principal directions carry a deliberately constructed classification rule, even when that rule is uncorrelated with the original semantic labels.

record.problems: Random-label results are presented as learning curves without numeric convergence times or terminal training-error values in the text. The paper does not report test error for these random-label comparisons or assess whether training hyperparameters were held fixed across label conditions.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying rows omitted. The paper's other results concern PC-bias, learning order, early stopping, or spectral bias and do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error on completely random labels in standard deep networks, chance test error, and unchanged training hyperparameters. Appendix D.1 describes validation-based hyperparameter searches for each experimental setup.
The numerical random-to-true-label training-time factor on natural images, a sweep over corrupted-label fractions, and applicability of the direct random-label comparison to nonlinear deep networks.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs to zero training error.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across a label-corruption sweep.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy labels. Separate convergence comparisons and PC-order results do not establish this temporal sequence.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text contains figure captions but no readable plotted values. No terminal accuracies or training-time ratios can be inferred from them. Missing measurements are listed as untested rather than treated as evidence against a version.

versions.untested_parts: The paper compares convergence with original and shuffled labels, but does not report whether random labels reach zero or near-zero training error, test error at chance, or the unchanged-architecture-and-hyperparameter condition.
Learning curves compare convergence qualitatively, but the text gives no small constant-factor training-time comparison or systematic sweep over fractions of corrupted labels.
No unstructured input conditions are tested.
No sweep from clean labels through partial corruption to all-random labels is reported.
No comparison of weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or their removal under random labels is reported.
The paper does not compare the order of learning real patterns and random labels as a function of training time.

rows.subject: two-layered linear networks
rows.operation_detail: Trained on cats and dogs data with original versus shuffled labels; compared learning curves.
rows.value: shuffled labels: figure only; convergence slower
rows.note: The text explicitly says the linear networks converge slower with random labels, but the figure-only curves provide no numeric factor or explicit training-error endpoint.
rows.check: The text establishes slower convergence with shuffled labels, but supplies no readable time ratio establishing V2's small constant factor. Remove V1: neither near-zero training error nor chance test error is established. The qualitative slowdown is valid evidence for V2's directional component.

rows.subject: two-layered linear networks
rows.operation_detail: Trained on ZCA-whitened cats and dogs data with original versus shuffled labels; compared learning curves.
rows.value: shuffled labels: figure only; rate described as identical
rows.note: The text states that convergence rate is identical for original and shuffled labels after whitening.
rows.check: Identical convergence rates support V2's optimization-ease component; 'absent' incorrectly treats the absence of a slowdown as absence of easy optimization. Equality also qualifies the slowdown component. Remove V1 because the required training-error endpoint is not established.

rows.subject: st-VGG networks
rows.operation_detail: Trained on datasets made linearly separable using the first P principal components; compared learning curves for P=10, 50, 500.

conditions.value: modified labels correlated with original labels

rows.value: For each P, text says lower P is learned faster; figure-only curves
rows.note: Training accuracy is the measure, but the text supplies only a qualitative comparison and no terminal accuracy values.
rows.check: These labels are constructed to be linearly separable in the first P principal components, rather than randomly corrupted labels. The result measures dependence on discriminative input directions. Section 6 reports 10 networks, whereas Appendix D.1 reports 100 for Figure 10; the ensemble size is internally inconsistent.

rows.subject: st-VGG networks
rows.operation_detail: Trained on datasets made linearly separable using the first P principal components, starting from shuffled labels; compared learning curves for P=10, 50, 500.

conditions.value: shuffled-derived labels uncorrelated with original labels

rows.value: For each P, text says lower P is learned faster; figure-only curves
rows.note: The authors say whether labels are real or shuffled makes little qualitative difference in these constructed settings; no terminal training accuracy or time factor is given.
rows.check: Starting labels are shuffled, but labels misclassified by a fitted linear separator are then switched. The resulting labels contain a designed learnable rule and are not completely random labels. Lack of correlation with original labels does not establish random labeling. The Figure 10 ensemble size is internally inconsistent between Section 6 and Appendix D.1.
